claim: The fly eye contains a random mosaic of photoreceptors defined by expression of light-detecting Rhodopsin proteins.
source: The fly eye, like the human eye, contains a random mosaic of photoreceptors defined by expression of light-detecting Rhodopsin proteins (Montell et al., 1987; Bell et al., 2007; Johnston and Desplan, 2010; Viets et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research

claim: Stochastic on/off expression of Spineless (Ss) determines R7 photoreceptor subtypes in flies.
source: In flies, the stochastic on/off expression of Spineless (Ss), a PAS-bHLH transcription factor, determines R7 photoreceptor subtypes.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Ss expression in R7s induces 'yellow' (yR7) fate and expression of Rhodopsin4 (Rh4).
source: Ss expression in a random subset of R7s induces 'yellow' (yR7) fate and expression of Rhodopsin4 (Rh4), whereas the absence of Ss in the complementary subset of R7s allows for 'pale' (pR7) fate and Rhodopsin3 (Rh3) expression (Figure 1A) (Wernet et al., 2006; Johnston et al., 2011; Thanawala et al., 2013; Johnston and Desplan, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations and Figure 1A showing the relationship between Ss expression and photoreceptor subtypes

claim: The absence of Ss in R7s allows for 'pale' (pR7) fate and Rhodopsin3 (Rh3) expression.
source: Ss expression in a random subset of R7s induces 'yellow' (yR7) fate and expression of Rhodopsin4 (Rh4), whereas the absence of Ss in the complementary subset of R7s allows for 'pale' (pR7) fate and Rhodopsin3 (Rh3) expression (Figure 1A) (Wernet et al., 2006; Johnston et al., 2011; Thanawala et al., 2013; Johnston and Desplan, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations and Figure 1A

claim: The on/off state of Ss in R7 indirectly determines the subtype fate of the neighboring R8 photoreceptor.
source: The on/off state of Ss in a given R7 also indirectly determines the subtype fate of the neighboring R8 photoreceptor.
evidence: Supported by subsequent explanation and citations

claim: pR7s lacking Ss signal to pR8s to activate expression of blue-detecting Rhodopsin5 (Rh5).
source: pR7s lacking Ss signal to pR8s to activate expression of blue-detecting Rhodopsin5 (Rh5). yR7s expressing Ss do not send this signal, resulting in expression of green-detecting Rhodopsin6 (Rh6) in yR8s (Figure 1A) (Franceschini et al., 1981; Montell et al., 1987; Zuker et al., 1987; Chou et al., 1996; Huber et al., 1997; Chou et al., 1999a; Mikeladze-Dvali et al., 2005; Mazzoni et al., 2008; Vasiliauskas et al., 2009; Jukam and Desplan, 2011; Hsiao et al., 2013; Johnston, 2013; Jukam et al., 2013; Jukam et al., 2016; Yan et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations and Figure 1A

claim: yR7s expressing Ss do not send a signal to R8s, resulting in expression of green-detecting Rhodopsin6 (Rh6) in yR8s.
source: pR7s lacking Ss signal to pR8s to activate expression of blue-detecting Rhodopsin5 (Rh5). yR7s expressing Ss do not send this signal, resulting in expression of green-detecting Rhodopsin6 (Rh6) in yR8s (Figure 1A) (Franceschini et al., 1981; Montell et al., 1987; Zuker et al., 1987; Chou et al., 1996; Huber et al., 1997; Chou et al., 1999a; Mikeladze-Dvali et al., 2005; Mazzoni et al., 2008; Vasiliauskas et al., 2009; Jukam and Desplan, 2011; Hsiao et al., 2013; Johnston, 2013; Jukam et al., 2013; Jukam et al., 2016; Yan et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations and Figure 1A

claim: The stochastic decision to express Ss is made cell-autonomously at the level of the ss gene locus via a random repression mechanism.
source: The stochastic decision to express Ss is made cell-autonomously at the level of the ss gene locus via a random repression mechanism.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: The R7/R8 enhancer induces ss expression in all R7s.
source: The R7/R8 enhancer induces ss expression in all R7s, whereas two silencer regions (silencer 1 and 2) repress expression in a random subset of R7s (Figure 1B) (Johnston and Desplan, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation and Figure 1B showing the ss locus structure

claim: Two silencer regions (silencer 1 and 2) repress ss expression in a random subset of R7s.
source: The R7/R8 enhancer induces ss expression in all R7s, whereas two silencer regions (silencer 1 and 2) repress expression in a random subset of R7s (Figure 1B) (Johnston and Desplan, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation and Figure 1B

claim: In most lab stocks, Ss is on in ~65% of R7s and off in ~35%.
source: In most lab stocks, Ss is on in ~65% of R7s and off in ~35% (Figure 1C) (Wernet et al., 2006; Johnston and Desplan, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations and Figure 1C showing stochastic distribution

claim: The proportion of SsON to SsOFF R7s varies greatly among fly lines derived from the wild.
source: Here, we find that the proportion of SsON to SsOFF R7s varies greatly among fly lines derived from the wild.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: A genome-wide association study identified a single base pair insertion that increases the affinity of a DNA binding site for a transcriptional repressor, significantly reducing the SsON/SsOFF ratio.
source: We performed a genome-wide association study (GWAS) and identified a single base pair insertion that increases the affinity of a DNA binding site for a transcriptional repressor, significantly reducing the SsON/SsOFF ratio.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from GWAS and subsequent validation experiments

claim: The genetic variant changes the proportion of photoreceptor subtypes and alters the innate color preference of flies.
source: This genetic variant changes the proportion of photoreceptor subtypes and alters the innate color preference of flies.
evidence: Supported by behavioral assay data presented in the manuscript

claim: Expression of Rh4 and Rh3 faithfully reports Ss expression in R7s (SsON = Rh4; SsOFF = Rh3).
source: We evaluated Rh4 and Rh3 expression, as they faithfully report Ss expression in R7s (i.e. SsON = Rh4; SsOFF = Rh3) (Figure 1A) (Thanawala et al., 2013; Johnston and Desplan, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations and Figure 1A

claim: The lab stock expressed Ss (Rh4) in 62% of R7s under hemizygous conditions.
source: While the lab stock expressed Ss (Rh4) in 62% of R7s under these conditions, expression among the DGRP lines varied significantly, ranging from 19% to 83% SsON (Rh4) (Figure 1E–F; Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E-F

claim: Expression of Ss among DGRP lines varied significantly, ranging from 19% to 83% SsON (Rh4).
source: While the lab stock expressed Ss (Rh4) in 62% of R7s under these conditions, expression among the DGRP lines varied significantly, ranging from 19% to 83% SsON (Rh4) (Figure 1E–F; Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E-F and source data

claim: A genome-wide association study identified a single base pair insertion within the ss locus ('ss insertion' or 'sin') that was significant (p<10−13) after Bonferroni correction.
source: We performed an association analysis and identified a single base pair insertion within the ss locus ('ss insertion' or 'sin') that was significant (p<10−13) after Bonferroni correction (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by GWAS data shown in Figure 1G

claim: sin was enriched in DGRP lines with a low ratio of SsON to SsOFF R7s.
source: sin was enriched in DGRP lines with a low ratio of SsON to SsOFF R7s (Figure 1F and H).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1F and H

claim: Naturally derived lines from Africa that are homozygous for sin displayed a decrease in the proportion of SsON (Rh4) R7s compared to lines from Africa lacking sin.
source: Naturally derived lines from Africa that are homozygous for sin displayed a decrease in the proportion of SsON (Rh4) R7s compared to lines from Africa lacking sin (Figure 1I) (Lack et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1I

claim: A lab stock balancer chromosome (TM6B) containing sin displayed a decrease in the proportion of SsON (Rh4) R7s when ss was hemizygous.
source: We identified sin on a balancer chromosome (TM6B) in a lab stock that similarly displayed a decrease in the proportion of SsON (Rh4) R7s when ss was hemizygous (Figure 1J).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1J

claim: Flies hemizygous for CRISPR sin alleles displayed a significant decrease in the proportion of SsON (Rh4) R7s.
source: To definitively test the role of sin, we used CRISPR to insert sin into a lab stock. Flies hemizygous for CRISPR sin alleles displayed a significant decrease in the proportion of SsON (Rh4) R7s (Figure 1K).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from CRISPR-mediated insertion shown in Figure 1K

claim: Flies homozygous for CRISPR sin alleles displayed a significant decrease in the proportion of SsON R7s as assessed by Ss antibody staining.
source: Using a Ss antibody, we examined Ss expression directly and found that flies homozygous for CRISPR sin alleles displayed a significant decrease in the proportion of SsON R7s (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–B and E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: sin causes a decrease in the ratio of SsON to SsOFF R7s.
source: Thus, sin causes a decrease in the ratio of SsON to SsOFF R7s.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple experimental validations

claim: The absorption spectra of Rh3 and Rh4 significantly overlap in the UV range.
source: The absorption spectra of Rh3 and Rh4 significantly overlap in the UV range (Feiler et al., 1992), complicating behavioral assessment of color preference caused by differences in R7 photoreceptor ratios.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: Rh5 and Rh6 in R8 photoreceptors have more distinct absorption spectra than Rh3 and Rh4.
source: Instead, we focused on the perception of blue light by Rh5 and green light by Rh6 in the R8 photoreceptors, as these Rhodopsins have more distinct absorption spectra (Salcedo et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: R8 fate is coupled to R7 fate.
source: Because R8 fate is coupled to R7 fate (Chou et al., 1996) (Figure 1A), we predicted that flies with sin would have a low ratio of Rh6- to Rh5-expressing R8s and would consequently prefer blue light, while flies without sin would have a higher ratio of Rh6- to Rh5-expressing R8s and would instead prefer green light.
evidence: Supported by citation and Figure 1A

claim: DGRP lines containing sin preferred blue light.
source: Indeed, DGRP lines containing sin preferred blue light, while DGRP lines lacking sin preferred green light (Figure 2A–C; Figure 2—source data 1), showing that sin changes innate color preference in flies.
evidence: Supported by behavioral assay data shown in Figure 2A-C

claim: DGRP lines lacking sin preferred green light.
source: Indeed, DGRP lines containing sin preferred blue light, while DGRP lines lacking sin preferred green light (Figure 2A–C; Figure 2—source data 1), showing that sin changes innate color preference in flies.
evidence: Supported by behavioral assay data shown in Figure 2A-C

claim: sin changes innate color preference in flies.
source: Indeed, DGRP lines containing sin preferred blue light, while DGRP lines lacking sin preferred green light (Figure 2A–C; Figure 2—source data 1), showing that sin changes innate color preference in flies.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from behavioral assay data

claim: sin is a single base pair insertion within a previously uncharacterized non-coding region of the ss locus located ~7 kb upstream of the transcriptional start.
source: sin is a single base pair insertion within a previously uncharacterized non-coding region of the ss locus located ~7 kb upstream of the transcriptional start (Figure 1B and Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by genomic location data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 3A

claim: sin lies in a predicted binding site for the zinc finger transcription factor Klumpfuss (Klu), the fly homolog of Wilms' Tumor Suppressor Protein 1 (WT1).
source: sin lies in a predicted binding site for the zinc finger transcription factor Klumpfuss (Klu), the fly homolog of Wilms' Tumor Suppressor Protein 1 (WT1) (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) (Klein and Campos-Ortega, 1997; Yang et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by motif analysis shown in Figure 3B and citations

claim: The Klu binding site region is perfectly conserved across 21 Drosophila species covering 50 million years of evolution.
source: This region is perfectly conserved across 21 Drosophila species covering 50 million years of evolution, consistent with a critical regulatory role (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: Supported by conservation analysis shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B-C

claim: The number of reads containing the Klu binding site with sin (CGCCCACACC) was significantly higher than without sin (CGCCCACACA) in SELEX-seq data.
source: The number of reads containing the Klu binding site with sin (CGCCCACACC) was significantly higher than without sin (CGCCCACACA) (Figure 3D), and thus, Klu binds the endogenous ss sequence with sin better than without it.
evidence: Supported by SELEX-seq analysis shown in Figure 3D

claim: Klu binds the endogenous ss sequence with sin better than without it.
source: The number of reads containing the Klu binding site with sin (CGCCCACACC) was significantly higher than without sin (CGCCCACACA) (Figure 3D), and thus, Klu binds the endogenous ss sequence with sin better than without it.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from SELEX-seq data analysis

claim: 506 10-mers (0.10%) have frequencies greater than the Klu site without sin in SELEX-seq data.
source: Considering the frequency of 10-mers as a measure of site preference, we found that 506 10-mers (0.10%) have frequencies greater than the Klu site without sin, whereas only 366 10-mers (0.07%) have frequencies greater than the Klu site with sin.
evidence: Supported by SELEX-seq data analysis

claim: Only 366 10-mers (0.07%) have frequencies greater than the Klu site with sin in SELEX-seq data.
source: Considering the frequency of 10-mers as a measure of site preference, we found that 506 10-mers (0.10%) have frequencies greater than the Klu site without sin, whereas only 366 10-mers (0.07%) have frequencies greater than the Klu site with sin.
evidence: Supported by SELEX-seq data analysis

claim: sin increases the binding affinity of the Klu site in vitro.
source: Together, sin increases the binding affinity of the Klu site in vitro.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from SELEX-seq analysis

claim: The endogenous 10-mer core sequence in ss (CGCCCACACA) deviates from the optimal site (CGCCCACGCA) at position 8, causing a dramatic reduction in the affinity for the endogenous site.
source: The endogenous 10-mer core sequence in ss (CGCCCACACA) deviates from the optimal site (CGCCCACGCA) at position 8, causing a dramatic reduction in the affinity for the endogenous site (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by SELEX-seq analysis shown in Figure 3E

claim: sin in position 10 significantly decreases binding affinity for the optimal Klu site.
source: Interestingly, sin in position 10 significantly decreases binding affinity for the optimal site (compare CGCCCACGCA to CGCCCACGCC), whereas it increases affinity for the endogenous Klu site in ss (compare CGCCCACACA to CGCCCACACC) (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by SELEX-seq analysis shown in Figure 3E

claim: sin increases affinity for the endogenous Klu site in ss.
source: Interestingly, sin in position 10 significantly decreases binding affinity for the optimal site (compare CGCCCACGCA to CGCCCACGCC), whereas it increases affinity for the endogenous Klu site in ss (compare CGCCCACACA to CGCCCACACC) (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by SELEX-seq analysis shown in Figure 3E

claim: Klu binding affinity is dependent on the relationship between the bases in position 8 and 10.
source: Our analysis indicates that Klu binding affinity is dependent on the relationship between the bases in position 8 and 10.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from SELEX-seq analysis

claim: Klu preferentially interacts with the site with sin (C in position 10) over the site without sin (A in position 10) in the endogenous spineless locus (A in position 8).
source: This dependence reveals that Klu preferentially interacts with the site with sin (C in position 10) over the site without sin (A in position 10) in the endogenous spineless locus (A in position 8), in contrast to the general predictions of the PWM (preferred G in position eight and A in position 10).
evidence: Conclusion drawn from SELEX-seq analysis

claim: The Klu site in the endogenous locus is a low-affinity site.
source: These data suggest that the Klu site in the endogenous locus is a low-affinity site and that sin increases its affinity.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from SELEX-seq analysis

claim: Flies hemizygous for an optimal Klu site displayed a lower proportion of SsON R7s compared to wild type flies.
source: We used CRISPR to mutate the endogenous low-affinity Klu site (ACGCCCACACAC) to the predicted optimized high-affinity site (ACGCCCACGCAC) and observed a decrease in the proportion of SsON R7s similar to flies with sin (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from CRISPR-mediated mutagenesis shown in Figure 3F

claim: An optimized high-affinity Klu site causes a similar phenotype as sin.
source: The observation that an optimized high-affinity Klu site causes a similar phenotype as sin is consistent with the conclusion that sin increases the binding affinity for Klu.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from CRISPR mutagenesis experiment

claim: Klu/WT1 has been shown to be a transcriptional repressor in other systems.
source: Klu/WT1 has been shown to be a transcriptional repressor in other systems (Drummond et al., 1992; McDonald et al., 2003; Kaspar et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Klu was expressed in R7s in larval eye imaginal discs in a Gaussian distribution.
source: We found that Klu was expressed in R7s in larval eye imaginal discs in a Gaussian distribution (Figure 4A–B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1) (Wildonger et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A-B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: Increasing the levels of Klu in Klu-expressing cells caused a decrease in the proportion of SsON (Rh4) R7s.
source: Indeed, increasing the levels of Klu in Klu-expressing cells (klu > klu), all photoreceptors (eye > klu), or specifically in all R7s (R7 > klu) caused a decrease in the proportion of SsON (Rh4) R7s (Figure 4C–D; Figure 1—figure supplement 2C and E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C-D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2C and E

claim: Increasing the levels of Klu in all photoreceptors caused a decrease in the proportion of SsON (Rh4) R7s.
source: Indeed, increasing the levels of Klu in Klu-expressing cells (klu > klu), all photoreceptors (eye > klu), or specifically in all R7s (R7 > klu) caused a decrease in the proportion of SsON (Rh4) R7s (Figure 4C–D; Figure 1—figure supplement 2C and E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C-D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2C and E

claim: Increasing the levels of Klu specifically in all R7s caused a decrease in the proportion of SsON (Rh4) R7s.
source: Indeed, increasing the levels of Klu in Klu-expressing cells (klu > klu), all photoreceptors (eye > klu), or specifically in all R7s (R7 > klu) caused a decrease in the proportion of SsON (Rh4) R7s (Figure 4C–D; Figure 1—figure supplement 2C and E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C-D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2C and E

claim: The decrease in the SsON/SsOFF ratio upon increasing Klu levels mimicked the effect of sin.
source: This decrease in the SsON/SsOFF ratio upon increasing Klu levels mimicked the effect of sin, consistent with sin increasing the binding affinity for the Klu repressor.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from comparison of experimental results

claim: klu loss-of-function mutants displayed increases in the proportion of SsON (Rh4) R7s.
source: Conversely, klu loss-of-function mutants displayed increases in the proportion of SsON (Rh4) R7s (Figure 4E–F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E-F

claim: The proportion of SsON R7s increased in klu null mutants as assessed by Ss antibody staining.
source: We examined Ss expression directly and found that the proportion of SsON R7s increased in klu null mutants (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D–E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D-E

claim: The proportion of SsON R7s increased in klu mutant clones compared to wild type clones.
source: Moreover, we found that the proportion of SsON R7s increased in klu mutant clones compared to wild type clones (Figure 4G–I).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4G-I

claim: Klu is endogenously expressed at intermediate levels and acts cell-autonomously to determine Ss expression state.
source: As the proportion of SsON R7s increases specifically in klu mutant clones and decreases upon ectopic expression of Klu in R7s, we conclude that Klu is endogenously expressed at intermediate levels and acts cell-autonomously to determine Ss expression state.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from clone analysis and ectopic expression experiments

claim: The ratio of Ss on/off gene expression is controlled by both the level of Klu protein and the binding affinity of the Klu site.
source: Our data suggest that the ratio of Ss on/off gene expression is controlled by both the level of Klu protein and the binding affinity of the Klu site.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple experimental manipulations

claim: Flies with both increased levels of Klu and sin showed a significant additional reduction in the proportion of SsON R7s.
source: We generated flies with increased levels of Klu in a sin genetic background and observed a significant additional reduction in the proportion of SsON R7s (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D

claim: The sin phenotype was suppressed in klu mutant heterozygotes.
source: To further test the relationship between Klu levels and binding site affinity, we reduced klu gene dosage in flies with sin and found that the sin phenotype was suppressed in klu mutant heterozygotes (Figure 4J).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4J

claim: The binding affinity of the Klu site and levels of Klu protein determine the proportion of SsON R7s.
source: We conclude that sin increases Klu binding affinity and that the binding affinity of the Klu site and levels of Klu protein determine the proportion of SsON R7s.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple experimental manipulations

claim: sin is absent among diverse drosophilid species spanning millions of years of divergence.
source: sin appears to be a relatively new mutation in D. melanogaster populations. sin is absent among diverse drosophilid species spanning millions of years of divergence (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–C) and is segregating at an extremely low frequency among non-admixed African D. melanogaster lineages (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–F).
evidence: Supported by conservation analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B-C

claim: sin is segregating at an extremely low frequency among non-admixed African D. melanogaster lineages.
source: sin appears to be a relatively new mutation in D. melanogaster populations. sin is absent among diverse drosophilid species spanning millions of years of divergence (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–C) and is segregating at an extremely low frequency among non-admixed African D. melanogaster lineages (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–F).
evidence: Supported by population genetic data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A-F

claim: sin likely rose to intermediate frequencies following D. melanogaster's colonization of Europe about 10–15 thousand years ago.
source: sin likely rose to intermediate frequencies following D. melanogaster's colonization of Europe about 10–15 thousand years ago (Li and Stephan, 2006).
evidence: Inference based on population genetic data and citation

claim: sin continues to segregate at intermediate frequencies amongst North American populations.
source: sin continues to segregate at intermediate frequencies amongst North American populations (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–F), which were established within the last 150 years from mixtures of European and African populations (Bergland et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by population genetic data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A-F

claim: North American D. melanogaster populations were established within the last 150 years from mixtures of European and African populations.
source: sin continues to segregate at intermediate frequencies amongst North American populations (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–F), which were established within the last 150 years from mixtures of European and African populations (Bergland et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: sin did not deviate from genome-wide patterns in allele frequency differentiation and haplotype homozygosity analyses.
source: Curiously, sin did not deviate from genome-wide patterns (Figure 1—figure supplement 3G–J) suggesting that it might be selectively neutral in contemporary D. melanogaster populations.
evidence: Supported by population genetic analyses shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3G-J

claim: sin might be selectively neutral in contemporary D. melanogaster populations.
source: Curiously, sin did not deviate from genome-wide patterns (Figure 1—figure supplement 3G–J) suggesting that it might be selectively neutral in contemporary D. melanogaster populations.
evidence: Inference based on population genetic analyses

claim: Rhodopsins are G-protein coupled receptors (GPCRs).
source: Rhodopsins are G-protein coupled receptors (GPCRs), a class of proteins identified as a source of natural behavioral variation in worms, mice, and voles (Young et al., 1999; Yalcin et al., 2004; Bendesky et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by established scientific knowledge and citations

claim: GPCRs are a class of proteins identified as a source of natural behavioral variation in worms, mice, and voles.
source: Rhodopsins are G-protein coupled receptors (GPCRs), a class of proteins identified as a source of natural behavioral variation in worms, mice, and voles (Young et al., 1999; Yalcin et al., 2004; Bendesky et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Dramatic differences in Rhodopsin expression patterns exist across insect species.
source: Dramatic differences in Rhodopsin expression patterns across insect species (Hilbrant et al., 2014; Wernet et al., 2015) suggest that variation in the expression of GPCRs, rather than retinal morphology, may allow rapid evolution in response to environmental changes.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Variation in the expression of GPCRs, rather than retinal morphology, may allow rapid evolution in response to environmental changes.
source: Dramatic differences in Rhodopsin expression patterns across insect species (Hilbrant et al., 2014; Wernet et al., 2015) suggest that variation in the expression of GPCRs, rather than retinal morphology, may allow rapid evolution in response to environmental changes.
evidence: Inference based on cited research

claim: Low-affinity binding sites ensure the timing and specificity of gene expression.
source: Low-affinity sites ensure the timing and specificity of gene expression (Jiang and Levine, 1993; Gaudet and Mango, 2002; Scardigli et al., 2003; Rowan et al., 2010; Ramos and Barolo, 2013; Crocker et al., 2015; Farley et al., 2015; Crocker et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research

claim: The suboptimal Klu site, bound by endogenous levels of Klu, yields the normal 65:35 SsON/SsOFF ratio.
source: The suboptimal Klu site, bound by endogenous levels of Klu, yields the normal 65:35 SsON/SsOFF ratio.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental data

claim: Changing the affinity of the Klu site or the level of Klu alters the ratio of SsON/SsOFF cells.
source: Changing the affinity of the site or the level of Klu alters the ratio of SsON/SsOFF cells.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental manipulations

claim: Stochastic on/off gene expression is controlled by threshold levels of trans factors binding to low-affinity sites.
source: We conclude that stochastic on/off gene expression is controlled by threshold levels of trans factors binding to low-affinity sites.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental findings

claim: The level of Klu (analog input) determines the binary on/off ratio of Ss expression (digital output).
source: The level of Klu (analog input) determines the binary on/off ratio of Ss expression (digital output).
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental findings

claim: sin or genetic perturbation of klu affected the frequency of Ss expression but not levels.
source: Interestingly, sin or genetic perturbation of klu affected the frequency of Ss expression (Figures 1F, I–K and 4C–J, Figure 1—figure supplement 2) but not levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in multiple figures

claim: Conservation of additional base pairs surrounding the Klu site is consistent with cooperative binding of Klu and other factors.
source: Conservation of additional base pairs surrounding the Klu site (Figure 3C) is consistent with cooperative binding of Klu and others factors, possibly through dimerization or multimerization.
evidence: Inference based on conservation data shown in Figure 3C

claim: The regions encompassing and neighboring the Klu binding site drive gene expression in the eye.
source: The regions encompassing and neighboring the Klu binding site drive gene expression in the eye (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), suggesting that complex interactions between this regulatory DNA element, the R7/R8 enhancer, and the two silencers (Figure 1B) ultimately control the ss on/off decision.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: Complex interactions between the regulatory DNA element containing the Klu site, the R7/R8 enhancer, and the two silencers ultimately control the ss on/off decision.
source: The regions encompassing and neighboring the Klu binding site drive gene expression in the eye (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), suggesting that complex interactions between this regulatory DNA element, the R7/R8 enhancer, and the two silencers (Figure 1B) ultimately control the ss on/off decision.
evidence: Inference based on experimental data

claim: Fine tuning of binding site affinities and transcription factor levels will emerge as a common mechanistic feature that determines the ratio of alternative fates in stochastic systems.
source: We predict that fine tuning of binding site affinities and transcription factor levels will emerge as a common mechanistic feature that determines the ratio of alternative fates in stochastic systems.
evidence: Prediction based on findings from this study

claim: Stochastic fate specification diversifies sensory neuron subtypes in worms, flies, mice, and humans.
source: Stochastic fate specification diversifies sensory neuron subtypes in a wide array of species including worms, flies, mice, and humans (Ressler et al., 1993; Roorda and Williams, 1999; Troemel et al., 1999; Hofer et al., 2005; Johnston and Desplan, 2010; Magklara and Lomvardas, 2013; Alqadah et al., 2016; Viets et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research

claim: Levels of Ss expression were not significantly different between wild type and klu mutant SsON R7s.
source: Levels of Ss expression were not significantly different between wild type and klu mutant SsON R7s. A-C are from three representative retinas. ns indicates not significant, p>0.05.
